The shortest stopping distance is the one in which friction supplies its **maximum**
retarding force.
**Step 1 — find the retarding force.** On a horizontal road, N = mg, so the greatest
friction available is
f = μmg ✓
**Step 2 — find the deceleration.**
a = f/m = **μg**
independent of the mass ✓
**Step 3 — apply v² = u² − 2as, stopping from v₀.**
0 = v₀² − 2(μg)s
**s = v₀²/(2μg)** ✓
**The energy route, which is quicker.** All the kinetic energy must be dissipated by
friction over the stopping distance:
½mv₀² = μmg s
**s = v₀²/(2μg)** ✓ the same, with the mass cancelling as before.
**Why the mass does not matter.** A heavier car has more kinetic energy to lose, but it
also presses harder on the road and so generates proportionally more friction ✓ The two
effects cancel exactly - which is why a loaded lorry and a small car stop in about the
same distance on the same surface.
**Why the dependence on speed is so dangerous.** The distance goes as **v₀²** ✓ Doubling
the speed **quadruples** the stopping distance; tripling it makes the distance nine times
greater. This is the single most important fact behind speed limits.
**A worked value.** With μ = 0·5, g = 10 m s⁻² and v₀ = 20 m s⁻¹ (72 km/h):
s = 400/(2 x 0·5 x 10) = **40 m** ✓
and at 40 m s⁻¹ it would be **160 m** - four times as far.
**Why "shortest".** Braking harder than μmg makes the wheels **lock and skid**, and
sliding friction is lower than the limiting static value ✓ The minimum distance is
achieved by braking right at the threshold, which is what anti-lock braking systems are
designed to do.
**Reading the distractors.** **v₀²/μ** ✗ and **v₀/μg** ✗ fail on dimensions - the first
is not even a length. **v₀²/μg** ✗ has the right form but omits the factor **2** that
comes from ½mv² ✓
∴ v₀²/2μg.

Apply the work-energy theorem over the **whole** journey: the fall plus the penetration.
**Step 1 — note the two stages.**
falling freely through **h**, gaining kinetic energy
penetrating a depth **d**, losing all of it to the wood's resistance ✓
**Step 2 — write the energy balance over the whole motion.** The knife starts at rest and
ends at rest, so the total work done on it is **zero**:
work by gravity = work against resistance
mg(h + d) = R d
**Step 3 — solve for R.**
R = mg(h + d)/d
= **mg(1 + h/d)** ✓
**Why the total drop is h + d and not just h.** Gravity keeps acting while the knife
sinks into the wood, so it falls a further distance d ✓ Omitting it gives
R = mgh/d, a common and slightly low answer.
**Checking the formula's behaviour.**
if h = 0, the knife is merely placed on the wood: R = **mg** ✓ correct, since the wood
just supports its weight
if d is very small - a hard floor - R becomes **very large** ✓ which is why a knife
dropped on stone transmits a huge force and may chip.
**A worked value.** A 0·2 kg knife dropped from 2 m penetrating 1 cm:
R = (0·2)(9·8)(1 + 2/0·01)
= 1·96 x 201
= **394 N** ✓ about 200 times the knife's weight - a striking illustration of why a small
stopping distance means an enormous force.
**Why the answer does not involve time.** The work-energy theorem relates **forces and
distances**, sidestepping the duration of the impact entirely ✓ Attempting this with
Newton's second law would require the unknown impact time.
**Reading the distractors.** **mg** ✗ is the static case, h = 0. **mg(1 − h/d)** ✗ would
become **negative** for h > d, meaning the wood pulls the knife in - absurd.
**mg(1 + h)/d** ✗, as printed without the bracket round the whole, is dimensionally
unsound ✓
∴ mg(1 + h/d).

The two fragments carry **equal and opposite momenta**, and kinetic energy expressed
through momentum makes the ratio immediate.
**Step 1 — conserve momentum.** The particle is stationary before the explosion, so
m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ ✓
the two momenta are equal in magnitude, call it **p**.
**Step 2 — write the kinetic energy in terms of momentum.**
K = ½mv² = **p²/(2m)**
**Step 3 — take the ratio.** With the same p for both:
K₁/K₂ = [p²/(2m₁)]/[p²/(2m₂)]
= **m₂/m₁** ✓
**What this says.** Kinetic energy is shared **inversely** as the mass ✓ The **lighter**
fragment carries the **larger** share of the energy, though both carry the same momentum.
**A worked instance.** A 3 kg body explodes into 1 kg and 2 kg pieces, with momentum
6 kg m s⁻¹ each way:
1 kg piece: v = 6 m s⁻¹, K = **18 J**
2 kg piece: v = 3 m s⁻¹, K = **9 J** ✓
ratio K₁ : K₂ = 18 : 9 = 2 : 1 = m₂ : m₁ ✓ exactly as the formula gives.
**Why this matters in practice.** It is the reason a **rifle recoils gently** while the
bullet flies off with lethal energy ✓ Rifle and bullet share equal momentum, but the
bullet, being a thousand times lighter, takes a thousand times the energy. The same
principle governs rocket exhaust and alpha decay.
**The direct route, for comparison.**
K₁/K₂ = (½m₁v₁²)/(½m₂v₂²) = (m₁/m₂)(v₁/v₂)²
and from momentum conservation v₁/v₂ = m₂/m₁, so
K₁/K₂ = (m₁/m₂)(m₂/m₁)² = **m₂/m₁** ✓ the same answer, more laboriously.
**Reading the distractors.** **1** ✗ would mean equal sharing, true only for equal
masses. **m₁/m₂** ✗ has the ratio inverted - the commonest error, and it would make the
**heavier** fragment the faster. **m₁v₂/(m₂v₁)** ✗ simplifies to (m₂/m₁)² by momentum
conservation ✓
∴ m₂/m₁.

Gravity is a **conservative** force, so the work done against it depends only on the
height - and a smooth incline adds nothing else.
**Step 1 — identify the forces doing work.** On a **smooth** incline there is no
friction, so only **gravity** opposes the motion up the slope ✓
**Step 2 — compute the work against gravity.** For a slope of angle θ and length L, with
L sin θ = h:
W = (mg sin θ) x L
= mg(L sin θ)
= **mgh** ✓
The angle cancels: a long gentle slope needs a **small force over a long distance**, a
short steep one a **large force over a short distance**, and the products are equal.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The work is **mgh** whatever the inclination, so the statement is
**true always** ✓
**What a conservative force means.** The work it does depends only on the **endpoints**,
not on the path taken ✓ Gravity, the spring force and the electrostatic force are all
conservative; friction and air resistance are not.
**A worked comparison.** Raising 10 kg through 2 m, with g = 10:
**30° slope**: length 4 m, force mg sin 30° = 50 N, work = 50 x 4 = **200 J**
**60° slope**: length 2·31 m, force 86·6 N, work = 86·6 x 2·31 = **200 J**
**vertically**: force 100 N over 2 m = **200 J** ✓ all identical.
**What the incline does buy.** Not less work, but a smaller **force** ✓ That is the whole
purpose of a ramp as a simple machine: it trades distance for effort, leaving the energy
unchanged.
**The essential caveat.** This holds only because the plane is **smooth** ✓ With friction
the work becomes mgh + μmg cos θ x L, which **does** depend on the angle - a gentler
slope means a longer path and more energy lost to friction.
**Reading the distractors.** **False always** ✗ contradicts the conservative nature of
gravity. **Depends on several other factors** ✗ and **cannot predict** ✗ would be right
only if friction were present, which "smooth" excludes ✓
∴ True always.

Convert each unit to joules and compare.
**Step 1 — write each in joules.**
**erg** = 10⁻⁷ J
**electron volt** = 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ J
**calorie** = 4·186 J
**kilowatt hour** = (1000 W)(3600 s) = **3·6 x 10⁶ J** ✓
**Step 2 — rank them.**
eV (10⁻¹⁹) < erg (10⁻⁷) < calorie (4·19) < **kWh (3·6 x 10⁶)** ✓
The kilowatt hour is the largest by an enormous margin.
**The scale of the difference.** One kilowatt hour is
3·6 x 10⁶/1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = **2·25 x 10²⁵ electron volts** ✓
a span of twenty-five orders of magnitude between the smallest and largest unit on the
list.
**Where each unit is used, and why.**
**electron volt** - atomic and nuclear physics, where energies are tiny; the energy an
electron gains across one volt ✓
**erg** - the CGS unit, now largely historical
**calorie** - heat and nutrition; the energy to warm 1 g of water by 1 °C
**kilowatt hour** - the commercial unit of electrical energy, the "unit" on an
electricity bill ✓
**A sense of a kilowatt hour.** It runs a 100 W bulb for **ten hours**, or boils about
**ten litres** of water from room temperature ✓ That is why it is the unit a power
company bills in - the joule would be absurdly small for the purpose.
**Why the unit chosen matters.** Each is sized to the phenomenon it describes ✓ Quoting
an electron's binding energy in kilowatt hours, or a monthly electricity bill in
electron volts, would be technically correct and practically useless.
**Reading the distractors.** **Calorie** ✗ is the second largest, but smaller than a
kilowatt hour by nearly a million. **Erg** ✗ and **electron volt** ✗ are the two
smallest ✓ Converting everything to joules before comparing is the only safe method.
∴ kilowatt hour.
